# Colorado Rolls Back Landmark AI Governance Law

Colorado lawmakers scaled back what was once considered the nation's most aggressive state artificial intelligence governance law, narrowing its scope and delaying enforcement another year after months of pressure from businesses and technology groups.

Gov. Jared Polis earlier this month signed a bill rewriting major portions of Colorado's landmark 2024 AI Act just weeks before the original framework was scheduled to take effect. The revised law delays implementation until Jan. 1, 2027 and removes several of the governance and compliance obligations that had drawn criticism from industry organizations preparing for the rollout.

The overhaul marks a shift for a law that had positioned Colorado at the center of the national debate over how states should regulate AI systems used in employment, lending, healthcare, insurance, housing and education decisions.

Colorado's original AI Act established a cross-sector regulatory framework governing "high-risk" AI systems. The law imposed requirements tied to risk management, annual impact assessments, documentation practices and efforts to mitigate algorithmic discrimination. Business groups and employers warned the framework created unclear compliance expectations and could sweep in relatively common workplace and operational AI tools.

The revised legislation abandons much of the original "high-risk AI system" structure and focuses more narrowly on automated decision-making tools used in consequential consumer-facing determinations.

Under the amended framework, organizations using covered AI systems will still need to notify consumers when automated systems play a role in significant decisions and provide mechanisms allowing individuals to seek human review or challenge outcomes.

The updated law also narrows several definitions surrounding algorithmic discrimination and removes portions of the original framework that would have required broader enterprise governance and documentation programs.

Colorado lawmakers had already delayed implementation once before after organizations raised concerns surrounding definitions, compliance timelines and uncertainty over how regulators would interpret portions of the law.

Several states including California, Illinois and New York have pursued narrower AI bills focused on issues such as deepfakes, biometric technologies and hiring discrimination. Colorado's original law was one of the first attempts to regulate enterprise AI governance practices more directly across multiple sectors at the state level.

The amended law preserves enforcement authority through the Colorado attorney general's office while maintaining certain recordkeeping and disclosure obligations for organizations using covered automated systems. Businesses deploying AI-assisted decision-making tools will likely still need to document how those systems are used in consequential determinations and ensure consumers retain meaningful avenues for human review.

The revisions also come as federal regulators continue debating how to properly secure and safeguard the public against potential threats posed by frontier AI systems. President Donald Trump recently scrapped an executive order aimed at creating a federal review process for frontier models over concerns it could hinder U.S. innovation in the AI sector (see: White House Faces Pressure to Rewrite AI Order ).
